The difference between Slack at its best and at its worst often comes down to how you handle **notifications**. A well-tuned notification setup lets you stay connected to what matters, without drowning in everything else. It helps you focus when you need to, catch up when you're ready, and avoid the noise that makes team communication feel fragmented.

This chapter explains how to take control. You’ll learn how to adjust notifications on your desktop and mobile, set up **Do Not Disturb** mode, mute channels or keywords, and choose between **mention notifications** and general ones. By the end, you’ll know how to use Slack without letting it use you.

---

## Understanding Slack Notifications: The Basics

Before you customize anything, it helps to understand what a notification actually is in Slack.

A **notification** is a signal—like a sound, a banner on your screen, or a vibration—that alerts you to a new message, reaction, or update in Slack. Notifications can come from:
- A **channel** you’re part of (like #marketing-launch)
- A **Direct Message (DM)** from a teammate
- A **thread** you’re following
- A keyword you’ve set up to watch (like your name or project code)

When you first join Slack, notifications are often set to “all” mode—meaning every message, even general ones in busy channels, can trigger an alert. For many people, this quickly leads to overload.

Think of it like a loudspeaker in an open office. If everything is announced all the time, you can’t focus. But if only urgent things are announced, you can work without jumping every time someone says “hi.”

Slack offers several ways to control what gets through:
- **Mention notifications** (only when you’re directly addressed with an **@mention**)
- **All notifications** (every new message in a channel)
- **No notifications** (muted channels)
- **Do Not Disturb** (a global pause on alerts)

---

## Adjusting Notification Settings on Desktop

Let’s start with your computer—where many people spend most of their workday.

### Where to Change Settings

1. Click your **profile picture** in the top-right corner of the Slack app.
2. Select **Preferences** from the menu.
3. Choose **Notifications** in the left sidebar.

This is your control center for all things alert-related.

### Choosing Notification Types

Slack lets you control how you’re notified, not just *if* you’re notified.

You’ll see options like:
- **Sound**
- **Banner** (a pop-up notification on your screen)
- **Badge app icon** (a red number on the Slack icon)
- **Email** (optional backup alerts)

You can turn each on or off based on your preference. For example:
- Keep **Sound** and **Banner** on for urgent messages
- Turn off **Badge app icon** if it’s distracting
- Disable **Email** if you want all alerts within Slack

> 💡 Tip: If you’re in a shared workspace or library, lower your **Sound** volume or set it to “Only when my sound is unmuted” to avoid embarrassing beeps.

### Setting Notification Preferences per Channel

Not all channels are equal. Some are critical (like #engineering-updates), others are optional (like #watercooler-chat).

To adjust notifications for a specific channel:
1. Open the channel.
2. Click the channel name at the top.
3. Select **Notification preferences**.
4. Choose:
   - **All new messages** (you’ll get alerts for every message)
   - **Only @mentions and keywords** (you’ll only get alerts when someone tags you)
   - **Nothing** (mute the channel entirely)

> 🔍 Example: You might want **All new messages** for #marketing-launch, but **Only @mentions** for #random-ideas.

This way, you stay in the loop for important discussions without being pestered by every joke or meme.

---

## Customizing Notifications on Mobile

Your phone is always with you—and that’s exactly why it can be the biggest source of notification overload.

### Mobile Notification Settings

On your phone:
1. Open the Slack app.
2. Tap your **profile picture** in the top-left.
3. Go to **Settings** > **Notifications**.

You’ll see similar options to desktop:
- **Sound**
- **Vibration**
- **Badge app icon**
- **Push notifications** (alerts when the app is closed)

### Managing Channel Notifications on Mobile

In the mobile app, you can also adjust per-channel settings:
1. Open the channel.
2. Tap the channel name at the top.
3. Select **Notification preferences**.
4. Choose:
   - **All new messages**
   - **Only @mentions**
   - **Mute channel**

> 📱 Pro Tip: If you’re worried about missing something important overnight, set mobile notifications to **Only @mentions** and check channels in the morning. This prevents late-night pings from waking you up.

---

## Muting Channels and Keywords

Sometimes, a channel is useful—but only occasionally. Or you want to watch for a specific word without being alerted to every message.

### Muting a Channel

To mute a channel entirely:
- **Desktop**: Click the channel name > **Notification preferences** > **Nothing**
- **Mobile**: Tap channel name > **Notification preferences** > **Mute**

Once muted:
- You won’t get any notifications
- The channel remains in your sidebar
- You can still check it when you want

> ✅ Use Case: Mute #event-planning if you’re not involved—you can still peek in when needed, but it won’t ping you constantly.

### Setting Up Keyword Alerts

Want to be notified only when someone mentions a specific word—like your name, a project code, or a client’s brand?

1. Go to **Preferences** > **Notifications**
2. Under **My Keywords**, add words or phrases (e.g., “Alex”, “Q3 Launch”, “Client X”)
3. Choose whether to be notified via **push**, **email**, or **both**

Now, you’ll only get alerts when those words appear—great for staying aware without noise.

> ⚠️ Caution: Don’t overdo keywords. Too many can create the same overload you’re trying to avoid.

---

## Do Not Disturb: Your Focus Mode

One of the most powerful tools in Slack is **Do Not Disturb (DND)**.

DND is like putting a “Do Not Disturb” sign on your digital door. When it’s on:
- All notifications are paused
- You can still send and receive messages
- People see a “Do Not Disturb” status next to your name
- You can set exceptions for urgent messages

### Turning On Do Not Disturb

#### On Desktop:
- Click your **profile picture** > **Pause notifications**
- Choose a duration: 30 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours, or until tomorrow

#### On Mobile:
- Swipe right from the left edge of the screen to open the sidebar
- Tap **Pause notifications**
- Select a time limit

> ✨ Feature: On desktop, you can also set **Scheduled Do Not Disturb** to automatically pause alerts during focus hours, like 6 PM to 8 AM.

### Allowing Exceptions

Even during DND, you might want to allow critical messages. You can set exceptions:
1. Go to **Preferences** > **Notifications**
2. Under **Do Not Disturb**, choose:
   - **Allow only mentions and reactions**
   - **Allow direct messages and mentions**
   - **Allow all messages**

This ensures that if your manager or client sends a critical **@mention**, you’ll still be alerted—even if you’re in DND.

> 🧠 Scenario: You’re in a meeting from 2 to 3 PM. You set DND for 1 hour. During that time, only **@mentions** from your boss will ping your phone. Everyone else’s messages wait until you’re free.

---

## Mention Notifications vs. All Notifications

This is a key distinction that trips up many beginners.

| Type | What You Get | Best For |
|------|---------------|--------|
| **All notifications** | Alerts for every new message in a channel | Important channels where you’re actively involved |
| **Only @mentions** | Alerts only when someone tags you directly | Less critical channels or high-volume spaces |
| **Muted** | No alerts at all | Optional or social channels |

> 💬 Example: In a busy channel like #general, you might set it to **Only @mentions** so you’re not interrupted by every “Good morning!” or “Anyone seen the printer?”

Using **mention-only** mode in high-traffic channels keeps you connected without the noise.

---

## Best Practices for a Clean Notification Setup

Here are some practical tips to keep your Slack experience smooth:

- **Start minimal**: Begin with **Only @mentions** in most channels, then increase to **All new messages** only for the most important ones.
- **Use DND during deep work**: Schedule it during meetings or focus blocks.
- **Review weekly**: Once a week, check your notification settings. Mute any channels you don’t need daily.
- **Use keywords wisely**: Track your name, project names, or client brands—but don’t add too many.
- **Keep mobile quiet at night**: Set mobile notifications to **Only @mentions** if you don’t want late-night pings.

> 🛠 Tool Tip: Slack’s **Activity Bar** (on the right side) shows recent notifications. Use it to scan missed messages during DND without opening every channel.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

Even with the best settings, things can go wrong. Here’s how to fix common problems:

| Problem | Likely Cause | Fix |
|-------|-------------|-----|
| No notifications at all | Do Not Disturb is on, or notifications are disabled | Check DND status and system notification permissions |
| Getting too many alerts | Channels set to “All new messages” or too many keywords | Adjust channel settings or keyword list |
| Not seeing a specific alert | Slack is running in the background or sound is off | Check system sound settings and Slack’s audio preferences |
| Notifications work on desktop but not mobile | Mobile app permissions or background refresh disabled | Enable push notifications in phone settings |

> 🔧 Tip: On iOS, go to **Settings** > **Slack** > **Notifications** and ensure “Allow Notifications” is on. On Android, check **App info** > **Notifications**.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Sample Setup

Let’s walk through a realistic example.

**Your Role**: Marketing Coordinator
**Channels**:
- #marketing-launch (high priority)
- #social-media (moderate)
- #random (low)
- #design-requests (medium)

**Setup**:
1. **#marketing-launch**: Set to **All new messages** (you’re leading this)
2. **#social-media**: Set to **Only @mentions**
3. **#random**: **Mute** (you only check occasionally)
4. **#design-requests**: Set to **All new messages** (you approve every post)
5. **Keywords**: Add your name (“Alex”) and project name (“Q3 Launch”)
6. **Do Not Disturb**: Schedule from 6 PM to 8 AM daily
7. **Mobile**: Set to **Only @mentions** except for direct messages

Now:
- You get full alerts for the two critical channels
- You’re only pinged in others when tagged
- You sleep and focus without interruptions
- You can still catch up on quieter channels when you’re ready

---

## Key Takeaways

- Notifications control what breaks your focus—and what doesn’t.
- Use **Only @mentions** in most channels to reduce noise.
- **Do Not Disturb** lets you block alerts during focused work or after hours.
- **Muting channels** removes notifications without leaving the workspace.
- **Keywords** let you track specific words without watching every post.
- Review and adjust settings regularly to keep Slack working for you, not against you.
- Start conservative with alerts—you can always increase later.

modules.title: Using Slack Integrations and Apps
modules.content:
## Why Integrations Make Slack Even More Powerful

Imagine you're leading the **marketing-launch** campaign for your team. You’ve set up a dedicated **channel** called `#marketing-launch` to keep everyone aligned. Messages fly back and forth: designers share mockups, copywriters draft messages, and the project manager tracks deadlines. But then:

- A designer uploads a design file to Google Drive and pastes a link into Slack. Team members click, wait for the browser to open, log in to Drive, and navigate to the file. It works, but it’s slow.
- Your next meeting is in 10 minutes. Someone suggests using Zoom. You open Zoom, schedule the meeting, then paste the invite link into Slack. Again, it *works*, but it’s extra steps.
- The project manager checks the deadline in Asana, then types it into Slack. More context switching. More time lost.

This is **fragmented communication**—the enemy of productivity. It slows down response times, creates attachment chaos, and forces people to juggle tools just to get work done.

Slack integrations and apps are designed to fix this. They let you bring the tools you already use *into* Slack—so you never have to leave. Instead of copying links, pasting invites, or switching windows, everything happens where you’re already communicating. That’s the power of an integration: **it turns Slack from a chat app into a central command center for your work**.

In this chapter, you’ll learn what integrations and apps are, how to install and use the most common ones, and how to manage them without cluttering your workspace. By the end, you’ll see how tools like **Google Drive**, **Zoom**, and **Asana** can live inside Slack—making your team faster, more organized, and less distracted.

---

## What Are Slack Integrations and Apps?

Before we dive into setup, let’s clarify the terms.

### Integrations vs. Apps: What’s the Difference?

In Slack’s ecosystem, the words *integration* and *app* are often used interchangeably—but they mean slightly different things.

- **Integration**: A connection between Slack and another service (like Google Drive or Zoom). It allows Slack to send or receive information from that service.
  - Example: When you link your Google account, you’re creating an integration so Slack can fetch files from Drive.
- **App**: A piece of software built to run *inside* Slack. It can be a standalone tool (like a polling app) or a bridge to an external service (like a Zoom bot).
  - Example: The Zoom app lets you start or join meetings directly from Slack without visiting the Zoom website.

Think of it this way: an **integration** is the bridge; an **app** is what you use to cross it.

Both are installed through Slack’s **App Directory**—a central marketplace where you can find thousands of tools from third-party developers. Some apps require you to sign in to another service (like Google or Trello). Others work entirely within Slack (like polling or reminders).

> 💡 **Jargon Alert**
> **Third-party** means developed by someone outside your company. Slack itself is made by Slack Technologies, but integrations and apps are made by other companies (like Google or Zoom).

---

## Why Use Integrations and Apps?

Here’s the core reason: **they save time and reduce friction**.

Every time you switch from Slack to another tool, you lose focus. Studies show it can take up to **23 minutes** to regain concentration after an interruption. Integrations help you stay in the flow.

Here’s how they help:

- **Centralize your tools**: Instead of checking email, Drive, Zoom, and Asana separately, you see updates from all of them in Slack.
- **Reduce manual work**: No more copying links or pasting meeting invites. Slack can fetch files, post updates, or trigger actions automatically.
- **Improve visibility**: When a file is updated in Drive, Slack can notify the team. When a task is completed in Asana, Slack shares the news.
- **Enhance collaboration**: Some apps let you edit documents, run polls, or approve requests—all without leaving Slack.

Let’s look at a few common scenarios where integrations shine.

---

### Scenario: The Overwhelmed Project Manager

**Alex** manages a product launch. Every day, they juggle:
- Design files in Google Drive
- Task updates in Asana
- Meetings in Zoom
- Status reports in Notion

Without integrations:
- Alex has to check each tool separately.
- They paste Drive links into Slack and hope people click them.
- They schedule Zoom meetings in the Zoom app, then send invites via email and Slack.
- Updates in Asana don’t automatically appear in Slack.

With integrations:
- Google Drive files appear as previews in Slack. Click to open—no login required.
- Asana tasks are posted in Slack when updated. Alex doesn’t have to manually announce them.
- Zoom meetings are scheduled and joined directly from Slack. The invite link is automatically posted.
- Notion pages are searchable and shareable in Slack.

Result? Alex saves **hours per week** and the team stays in sync.

---

## Installing and Configuring Common Integrations

Now that you understand the *why*, let’s walk through the *how*. We’ll cover three of the most widely used integrations: **Google Drive**, **Zoom**, and **Google Calendar**.

> 📌 **Note**: You’ll need admin or owner permissions in your Slack workspace to install most integrations. If you’re not an admin, you can still use many apps—just ask your workspace admin to install them for you.

---

### ### Installing Google Drive

Google Drive is one of the most popular file-sharing tools. Integrating it with Slack lets you:
- Preview Drive files directly in Slack
- Upload files from Drive to Slack with one click
- Get notifications when files are shared with the team

#### Step-by-Step Setup

1. **Go to the App Directory**
   In Slack, click the **Apps** button in the left sidebar (it looks like a puzzle piece). Then click **App Directory**.

2. **Search for Google Drive**
   Type “Google Drive” in the search bar. You’ll see the official **Google Drive for Slack** app.

3. **Click “Add to Slack”**
   You’ll be redirected to a Google sign-in page. This is normal—Slack needs permission to access your Drive.

4. **Sign in to Google**
   Choose the Google account you use for Drive. Slack will ask for permissions:
   - View and manage your Google Drive files and photos
   - View and manage the files in your Google Drive
   - Connect to your Google Account
   Click **Allow** to proceed.

5. **Choose Where to Post Updates**
   Slack will ask which **channel** or **direct message** should receive file-sharing updates.
   - Example: Post to `#marketing-launch` so the team sees when new designs are shared.
   - You can change this later.

6. **Done!**
   Once connected, you’ll see a confirmation. Now, when someone shares a Drive file in Slack, it will appear as a preview.

#### Using Google Drive in Slack

- **Upload a file from Drive**: Click the **paperclip icon** in a message box → **Google Drive** → select a file.
- **Preview a shared file**: If someone pastes a Drive link, Slack shows a preview. Click it to open.
- **Get notified of new shares**: If a Drive file is shared with the team, Slack posts a message in the chosen channel.

> ⚠️ **Privacy Note**
> Only people with access to the file in Drive can view it in Slack. Slack doesn’t store the file—it just shows a preview.

---

### ### Setting Up Zoom

Zoom is the go-to video conferencing tool for many teams. With the Zoom app, you can:
- Start or join meetings without leaving Slack
- Schedule meetings and get reminders in Slack
- See meeting details in channels

#### Step-by-Step Setup

1. **Go to the App Directory**
   In Slack, click **Apps** → **App Directory**.

2. **Search for Zoom**
   Find the official **Zoom for Slack** app.

3. **Click “Add to Slack”**
   You’ll be redirected to Zoom’s website.

4. **Sign in to Zoom**
   Use your Zoom account to log in. Slack and Zoom will now connect.

5. **Choose Your Slack Workspace**
   If you manage multiple Zoom accounts, select the right one. Click **Authorize**.

6. **Done!**
   The Zoom app is now installed. You’ll see a new **Zoom** section in your Slack sidebar.

#### Using Zoom in Slack

- **Start a meeting**: In any channel, type `/zoom` and press Enter. A new meeting starts immediately. Slack posts the invite link.
- **Join a meeting**: Click the Zoom link in any message or channel.
- **Schedule a meeting**: Type `/zoom schedule` and follow the prompts. Slack creates the meeting in Zoom and posts the details.
- **See upcoming meetings**: Click the **Zoom** app in your sidebar to see all scheduled meetings.

> 💡 **Pro Tip**
> Want to schedule a meeting for a specific channel? Type `/zoom schedule #project-x` to create a meeting just for that team.

---

### ### Integrating Google Calendar

Google Calendar keeps track of your meetings and deadlines. With the Google Calendar app, you can:
- Get Slack notifications for upcoming events
- Post calendar updates in channels
- See your schedule without leaving Slack

#### Step-by-Step Setup

1. **Go to the App Directory**
   Click **Apps** → **App Directory**.

2. **Search for Google Calendar**
   Find the **Google Calendar** app.

3. **Click “Add to Slack”**
   You’ll be redirected to Google.

4. **Sign in to Google**
   Choose the account with your calendar. Grant Slack permission to:
   - See, edit, create, and delete your Google Calendar events and reminders
   - View your calendar settings

5. **Choose Notification Settings**
   Slack will ask how you want to be notified:
   - **Direct messages**: Slackbot will send you reminders
   - **Channels**: Post updates to a specific channel (e.g., `#team-calendar`)
   - **No notifications**: Just connect the calendar without alerts

6. **Done!**
   Once connected, you’ll start receiving notifications.

#### Using Google Calendar in Slack

- **Get reminders**: Slackbot will message you before a meeting starts (e.g., “You have a meeting in 10 minutes: Marketing Sync”).
- **See your schedule**: Type `/gcal` in any channel to see your upcoming events.
- **Post calendar updates**: If an event is added or changed, Slack can post it to a channel.

> ⚠️ **Note**
> Slack only shows events from calendars you have access to. It doesn’t see private events unless shared.

---

## Setting Up Notifications for Project Updates

Many teams use tools like **Asana**, **Trello**, or **Jira** to track projects. Instead of checking each tool, you can get updates directly in Slack.

Let’s use **Asana** as an example.

### ### Installing Asana for Slack

1. **Go to the App Directory**
   Click **Apps** → **App Directory**.

2. **Search for Asana**
   Find the official **Asana for Slack** app.

3. **Click “Add to Slack”**
   You’ll be redirected to Asana.

4. **Sign in to Asana**
   Log in with your Asana account. Slack and Asana will connect.

5. **Choose a Channel for Updates**
   Slack will ask where to post task updates. Example: `#marketing-launch`

6. **Done!**
   Now, when a task is completed, commented on, or assigned, Slack posts the update.

#### Example Update in Slack

> 📢 **Asana update in #marketing-launch**
> **Task:** Finalize hero image for landing page
> **Status:** Completed
> **Assigned to:** Jamie
> **Link:** [View in Asana](https://asana.com)

This keeps the team informed without extra effort.

> 📌 **Tip**
> You can also use slash commands in Slack to interact with Asana:
> - `/asana create task "Write blog post" due tomorrow in #content-planning`
> - `/asana list my tasks`

---

## Managing Installed Apps and Integrations

As you add more apps, your workspace can get cluttered. Here’s how to keep it tidy.

---

### ### Where to See Your Installed Apps

1. Click **Apps** in the left sidebar.
2. Click **Installed apps** to see a list of everything you’ve added.
3. To remove an app, click the three dots (⋮) next to its name → **Remove app**.

> ⚠️ **Warning**
> Removing an app disconnects it from your workspace. You’ll need to reinstall it if you want to use it again.

---

### ### Checking Permissions

Some apps may ask for more permissions than you’re comfortable with. To review:

1. Go to **Apps** → **Installed apps**.
2. Click on an app.
3. Scroll to **Permissions** to see what it can access.
4. If you’re unsure, click **Remove app** to revoke access.

> 💡 **Best Practice**
> Only install apps you trust. Check the developer (e.g., “Google” or “Zoom”) and read reviews in the App Directory.

---

### ### Organizing Apps by Purpose

Use these strategies to keep your workspace clean:

- **Use channels for context**: Install an app in a specific channel if it’s only relevant there.
  - Example: Install the **Trello** app in `#product-dev`, not the whole workspace.
- **Use slash commands sparingly**: Too many commands can clutter the `/` menu. Stick to the ones you use daily.
- **Uninstall unused apps**: If you’re not using an app after a month, remove it.

> 📌 **Tip**
> You can also **pin important apps** to your sidebar for quick access.

---

## Using Slash Commands to Interact with Apps

Slash commands are shortcuts that start with `/` and let you interact with apps directly in Slack.

### How They Work

- Type `/` in any message box. A list of available commands appears.
- Type the command name (e.g., `/zoom`, `/gcal`, `/asana`) and follow the prompts.

### Common Slash Commands

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|--------|--------|--------|
| `/zoom` | Start or join a Zoom meeting | `/zoom` → starts a new meeting |
| `/zoom schedule` | Schedule a future meeting | `/zoom schedule "Team Sync" at 2pm` |
| `/gcal` | See your calendar | `/gcal` → shows today’s events |
| `/asana create task` | Create an Asana task | `/asana create task "Write docs" due Friday` |
| `/remind` | Set a reminder | `/remind @jamie "Review design" at 4pm` |

> 💡 **Pro Tip**
> You can use slash commands in **threads** and **direct messages**, not just channels.

---

## Best Practices for Using Integrations

Integrations are powerful—but they can also overwhelm your workspace if not used thoughtfully.

### Do:

- **Start small**: Install one integration at a time and measure its impact.
- **Use channels wisely**: Post updates in channels where the team will see them.
- **Set boundaries**: Turn off notifications for less important updates.
- **Train your team**: Make sure everyone knows how to use the new tools.

### Don’t:

- ❌ Install every app you see. Ask: *Does this save time or add value?*
- ❌ Post every update in every channel. Keep notifications relevant.
- ❌ Ignore permissions. Only grant access to trusted apps.
- ❌ Forget to clean up. Uninstall apps you no longer use.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

Even the best integrations can hiccup. Here’s how to fix common problems.

### ### “I installed the app but don’t see it working.”

- **Check the app’s channel**: Some apps only post to a specific channel. Make sure you set the right one during setup.
- **Verify permissions**: Go to **Apps** → **Installed apps** → check the app’s settings.
- **Restart Slack**: Sometimes the app needs a refresh.

### ### “I can’t find the slash command.”

- **Check spelling**: Slash commands are case-sensitive. `/zoom` works; `/Zoom` may not.
- **Look in the command list**: Type `/` to see all available commands.
- **Reinstall the app**: The command may not have loaded properly.

### ### “The app is posting too many updates.”

- **Adjust notification settings**: Go to the app’s settings and reduce alert frequency.
- **Change the channel**: Move updates to a less active channel.
- **Use threads**: Some apps let you post updates in threads instead of channels.

### ### “I get an error when signing in.”

- **Check your internet connection**.
- **Clear your browser cache** and try again.
- **Use a different browser** (Chrome, Firefox, Safari).
- **Contact support**: If the issue persists, reach out to the app’s support team or Slack Help.

---

## Real-World Example: The Fully Integrated Workspace

Let’s revisit **Alex**, the project manager from earlier. Now, their team’s workflow looks like this:

- **Designs**: Shared in Google Drive → previewed in Slack.
- **Tasks**: Updated in Asana → posted in `#marketing-launch`.
- **Meetings**: Scheduled with `/zoom schedule` → invite posted automatically.
- **Deadlines**: Tracked in Google Calendar → reminders sent to Alex via Slackbot.
- **Polls**: Created with `/poll` → results posted in the channel.

Alex no longer has to:
- Copy links between tools
- Send separate meeting invites
- Manually announce updates

The team stays focused, and work moves faster.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Slack **integrations** connect Slack to other tools (like Google Drive or Zoom).
- Slack **apps** are tools that run inside Slack, often using integrations.
- Integrations **centralize work**, reducing context switching and saving time.
- Common integrations include **Google Drive**, **Zoom**, **Google Calendar**, and **Asana**.
- Use the **App Directory** to install and manage apps.
- **Slash commands** let you interact with apps directly in Slack (e.g., `/zoom`, `/gcal`).
- Keep your workspace clean by **removing unused apps** and **limiting notifications**.
- Start with one integration, test it, and expand gradually.

By integrating the right tools, you’re not just using Slack—you’re building a **productivity multiplier** for your team.

modules.title: Organizing Your Workspace: Pins, Bookmarks, and Saved Items
modules.content:
## Why Your Slack Can Feel Like a Black Hole (And How to Fix It)

Imagine this: It’s 3:45 PM on a Friday. You’re wrapping up a project, and you need to find the final version of the client proposal. You remember it was shared in the #project-alpha channel, but when you scroll through, you’re met with hundreds of messages—some from weeks ago, others from just this morning. You type “proposal” into Slack’s search bar, but the results are buried under unrelated mentions of “proposal” in other contexts. By the time you finally locate the file, it’s 4:15 PM, and you’ve wasted half an hour digging through digital clutter.

Sound familiar? Slack is a **centralizing communication platform**, but without structure, it can quickly become as chaotic as **Email: The Slow, Overwhelming Champion**—fragmented, hard to search, and impossible to keep track of. The good news? Slack gives you tools to tame the chaos: **pins**, **bookmarks**, and **saved items**. These features help you **centralize communication** by keeping important messages, files, and links at your fingertips—no more scrolling through endless threads or re-asking teammates for the same file.

In this chapter, you’ll learn how to use these tools to turn Slack from a cluttered mess into a **productivity multiplier**. You’ll discover how to:
- **Pin** critical messages or files to a channel so they’re always visible.
- **Save** items to your personal bookmarks for quick access later.
- **Organize** your bookmarks into folders (or categories) to keep things tidy and searchable.

By the end, you’ll be able to find what you need in seconds—not minutes—freeing up time to focus on what matters most.

---

## The Three Pillars of Slack Organization

Before diving into the tools, let’s clarify the three key features we’ll cover:

1. **Pins**: Like sticky notes on a bulletin board, pins attach important messages or files directly to a channel or direct message (DM) so they’re visible to everyone in that space. Pins are **public** within the channel or DM.
2. **Bookmarks**: These are **private** items you save for yourself. You can bookmark messages, files, or links, and they’ll appear in your personal **Saved items** list.
3. **Saved items**: A centralized view of all your bookmarked items, accessible only to you. Think of it as your personal library of Slack resources.

These tools work together to keep your workspace clean and your workflow smooth. Let’s explore each one in detail.

---

## Pinning Important Messages and Files

Pins are your channel’s “top hits.” They sit at the top of a channel or DM, ensuring team members can’t miss them. Pins are ideal for:
- Project deadlines
- Key decisions or action items
- Links to shared resources (e.g., a design system or onboarding guide)
- Files that everyone needs (e.g., a budget spreadsheet or project timeline)

### How to Pin a Message or File

1. **Locate the item**: Find the message or file in the channel or DM.
2. **Hover over it**: Move your cursor over the message. A row of icons will appear.
3. **Click the pin icon**: It looks like a pushpin (📌). Select it.
4. **Confirm**: A pop-up will ask, “Pin this message?” Click **Pin**.

The item will now appear in the **Pinned items** section at the top of the channel or DM.

**Pro tip**: If you pin a file, Slack will show a preview. Hover over the file to see options like downloading or opening it in another app.

### Managing Pinned Items

To view or edit pinned items:
1. Open the channel or DM.
2. Click the **channel name** (or DM name) at the top.
3. Select **Pinned items** from the dropdown menu.

From here, you can:
- **Unpin** an item by hovering over it and clicking the pin icon again.
- **Add a note** to a pinned item (e.g., “Final client proposal—do not edit”).
- **Reorder** pinned items by dragging and dropping them.

**Scenario**: Your team is working on a product launch. The marketing lead pins the final product brief to the #marketing-launch channel. Now, every team member who joins the channel sees the brief first, reducing confusion and ensuring everyone is on the same page.

---

## Saving Items for Later with Bookmarks

Pins are great for teams, but what if you need to save something for **yourself**? That’s where **bookmarks** come in. Bookmarks let you save messages, files, or links to your personal **Saved items** list, which only you can see.

### What Can You Bookmark?

- **Messages**: Any text message in a channel or DM.
- **Files**: PDFs, images, spreadsheets, or documents shared in Slack.
- **Links**: URLs from the web or Slack channels (e.g., a design guide or a Google Doc).

### How to Bookmark an Item

1. **Find the item**: Locate the message, file, or link in Slack.
2. **Hover over it**: Click the three dots (⋯) that appear.
3. **Select “Save”**: This adds the item to your **Saved items**.

**Keyboard shortcut**: If you’re using Slack on desktop, you can press `Cmd + S` (Mac) or `Ctrl + S` (Windows) to bookmark an item.

### Accessing Your Saved Items

To view your bookmarks:
1. Click your **profile picture** in the top-right corner of Slack.
2. Select **Saved items** from the dropdown menu.

You’ll see a list of all your bookmarked items, organized by date.

---

## Organizing Your Bookmarks with Folders

By default, your **Saved items** list is a chronological feed. But if you bookmark a lot of items, it can get overwhelming. Slack lets you **organize your bookmarks into folders**, so you can group related items and find them faster.

### Creating a Folder

1. Open your **Saved items** list (click your profile picture > **Saved items**).
2. Click the **New folder** button in the top-right corner.
3. Give your folder a name (e.g., “Project Alpha,” “Design Resources,” “Meeting Notes”).
4. Click **Create**.

### Adding Items to a Folder

1. Open an item in your **Saved items** list.
2. Click the **folder icon** (📁) next to the item.
3. Select the folder you want to add it to.

**Tip**: You can also drag and drop items into folders directly from your **Saved items** list.

### Managing Folders

To rename, delete, or move folders:
1. Open your **Saved items** list.
2. Click the **three dots (⋯)** next to the folder name.
3. Select the action you want to take (e.g., **Rename**, **Delete**, or **Move items**).

**Scenario**: You’re part of three projects: Alpha, Beta, and Gamma. Instead of scrolling through 50 bookmarks, you create folders for each project. Now, when you need the Alpha project timeline, you open the “Project Alpha” folder and find it instantly.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Real-World Example

Let’s walk through a typical workflow where these tools shine:

**Step 1: Pin a critical update**
During a team meeting in #team-updates, your manager shares a deadline change for Project X. Instead of losing it in the conversation, you pin the message to the channel. Now, anyone who joins the channel sees the update first.

**Step 2: Bookmark a helpful resource**
Later, you find a link to a design tool tutorial in #design-talk. You bookmark it to your **Saved items** so you can revisit it later.

**Step 3: Organize with a folder**
You create a folder called “Design Resources” and move the tutorial link into it. Now, all your design-related bookmarks are in one place.

**Step 4: Use Saved items to prepare for a meeting**
The next day, you open your **Saved items** to review the Project X update (pinned) and the design tutorial (bookmarked). Everything you need is in one, organized place.

By combining pins, bookmarks, and folders, you’ve turned Slack from a chaotic mess into a **tidy and searchable** system.

---

## Pro Tips for Mastering Slack Organization

1. **Use pins for team-wide visibility**: Pins are public, so use them for items everyone in the channel needs to see.
2. **Bookmark everything useful**: Even if you don’t need it now, bookmark it. You’ll thank yourself later.
3. **Name folders descriptively**: Avoid vague names like “Stuff” or “Misc.” Use names like “Client Reports” or “Training Materials.”
4. **Review your Saved items regularly**: Every few weeks, open your **Saved items** and clean up outdated or irrelevant bookmarks.
5. **Combine with Slack’s search**: If you can’t find something in your bookmarks, use Slack’s search (`Cmd + K` or `Ctrl + K`) to locate it quickly.

---

## Common Pitfalls (And How to Avoid Them)

- **Over-pinning**: Don’t pin everything. Only pin items that are truly critical to the channel.
- **Creating too many folders**: Start with broad categories (e.g., “Projects,” “Resources”) and refine as you go.
- **Ignoring Saved items**: Bookmarks are useless if you never use them. Make it a habit to check your **Saved items** weekly.
- **Forgetting to unpin outdated items**: Old pins clutter your channel. Review them monthly and remove anything no longer relevant.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Pins** attach important messages or files to the top of a channel or DM for team-wide visibility.
- **Bookmarks** let you save items for yourself, keeping them in your personal **Saved items** list.
- **Folders** help you organize bookmarks into categories, making it easier to find what you need.
- Combine these tools to turn Slack from a chaotic space into a **centralized, tidy, and searchable** system.
- Regularly review your **Saved items** to keep them relevant and useful.

modules.title: Collaborating with Slack Huddles and Calls
modules.content:
## Why Slack Calls Beat Email (Again)

You're midway through a project when a teammate shares a file in a channel with the note: *"This design needs feedback ASAP."* Instead of starting a back-and-forth email thread that will take hours to resolve—or worse, a meeting that derails everyone’s schedule—you hit a single button and instantly hop on a voice call with three colleagues. No scheduling emails. No "Can you meet tomorrow at 3?" delays. Just immediate, focused discussion.

This is the power of **Slack Huddles and Calls**. They’re not just quick alternatives to email or calendar invites; they’re designed for the way modern teams actually work—fast, ad-hoc, and integrated into the flow of conversation. Whether you need a 30-second voice check-in or a 15-minute screen-sharing session, Slack’s calling features let you collaborate without leaving the app.

In this chapter, you’ll learn how to:
- Start a spontaneous voice call (a **Huddle**) from a channel or direct message
- Turn that voice call into a video call with one click
- Share your screen to show a document, design, or bug in real time
- Manage who’s in the call, mute participants, and control settings
- Use the call toolbar to adjust audio, video, and layout

No prior experience needed—just a Slack workspace and a willingness to talk instead of type.

---

## Starting a Slack Huddle: Quick Voice Chats in Seconds

A **Huddle** in Slack is a lightweight voice-only call that lets you talk to teammates without planning ahead. It’s perfect for:

- Quick clarifications: *"Can you confirm the client’s email address?"*
- Brainstorming: *"Let’s talk through the new feature outline."*
- Status updates: *"What’s the hold-up on the design?"*

You can start a Huddle from anywhere in Slack where you see teammates: a **channel**, a **direct message (DM)**, or even a **thread**.

### How to Start a Huddle

1. Open a channel or DM where your teammates are.
2. Look for the **phone icon** (📞) in the top-right corner of the message composer (the box where you type messages).
   - If you hover over it, it will say *"Start a Huddle."*
3. Click the icon. Slack will ring your teammates’ devices.
   - They’ll see a notification: *"[Your Name] started a Huddle in [Channel Name]."*

> 💡 **Pro Tip**: You don’t need to wait for everyone to answer. If someone’s away, Slack will keep trying in the background. You can still start the Huddle and talk to whoever joins.

### Joining a Huddle

When someone starts a Huddle, you’ll get a notification in:
- The channel or DM where it was started
- Your Slack notifications (if you have them enabled)
- The Slack desktop or mobile app

Just click **"Join"** to hop in.

> 📱 **Mobile Note**: On the Slack mobile app, the Huddle notification appears at the top of the screen. Tap it to join.

### What Happens During a Huddle?

Once you join:
- You’ll see a small floating window showing who’s in the call.
- You can mute/unmute yourself using the microphone button.
- The call stays active even if you switch to other Slack channels or messages.
- If someone joins late, they’ll hear the ongoing conversation.

But here’s the best part: **It’s ephemeral**. When no one is left in the Huddle, it automatically ends. No lingering calls, no accidental hang-ups.

---

## From Voice to Video: Upgrading to a Slack Call

A Huddle is great for quick chats, but sometimes you need to see faces or share visuals. That’s when you can **upgrade to a video call** with one click.

### Starting a Video Call from a Huddle

1. While in a Huddle, look for the **camera icon** (📹) in the call toolbar.
2. Click it. The call will switch to video, and your camera will turn on.
3. Everyone in the Huddle will automatically join the video call.

> ⚠️ **Note**: If your camera is off, Slack will ask permission to turn it on when you start the video call.

### Starting a Video Call Directly (Without a Huddle)

You don’t need to start with audio first. You can launch a video call directly:

1. In a channel or DM, click the **video camera icon** (📹) in the message composer.
2. Slack will ring your teammates with a video call invitation.
3. They can accept and join with their camera on.

> ✨ **Bonus**: Video calls in Slack also include screen-sharing capabilities—more on that soon.

### What You’ll See During a Video Call

- **Gallery view**: Shows all participants in small tiles.
- **Speaker view**: Focuses on the person currently talking.
- **Floating window**: Lets you move the call around your screen while you work.

You can switch between views by clicking the **layout icon** in the toolbar.

---

## Sharing Your Screen: Show, Don’t Tell

Sometimes, words aren’t enough. Whether you’re reviewing a design, debugging code, or walking through a spreadsheet, **screen sharing** turns your call into a live collaboration tool.

### How to Share Your Screen

1. During a video call or Huddle, look for the **screen icon** (🖥️) in the call toolbar.
2. Select **Share your entire screen** or **Share a window**.
   - **Entire screen**: Shows everything on your display (use this for full presentations).
   - **Window**: Lets you choose a specific app or browser tab to share (safer and less distracting).
3. Click **Share**. Slack will begin broadcasting your screen to everyone in the call.
4. To stop sharing, click the **screen icon** again and select **Stop sharing**.

> 🔒 **Privacy Tip**: Only share what you intend to. Close private emails or sensitive tabs before sharing your screen.

### Who Can Share Their Screen?

- **Hosts or presenters**: In some organizations, only certain roles can share screens by default.
- **Participants**: In most Workspaces, any attendee can share their screen unless settings restrict it.

> 💬 **Scenario**: You’re in a video call with your design team. Instead of describing a layout issue, you share your screen and point to the exact button that’s misaligned. The team fixes it on the spot.

---

## Managing Participants and Call Settings

Staying in control of your call ensures it stays productive and distraction-free. Here’s how to manage who’s involved and how the call behaves.

### Viewing and Controlling Participants

1. During a call, click the **people icon** (👥) in the toolbar.
2. A sidebar will open showing:
   - **Who’s in the call**
   - **Who’s talking** (highlighted in blue)
   - Options to **mute**, **remove**, or **pin** participants (if you have permissions)

> 🔤 **Jargon Alert**: **Pinning a participant** keeps their video tile visible even if they’re not speaking. Useful for presenters or key decision-makers.

### Muting and Unmuting

- Click the **microphone icon** to mute/unmute yourself.
- **For other participants**: In the participant list, hover over their name and click the **mute icon** (🔇) if you have permission.

> ⚠️ **Note**: Only Workspace admins or call hosts (depending on settings) can mute others.

### Adjusting Call Settings

Click the **three dots (⋯)** in the call toolbar to access:
- **Audio settings**: Choose your input/output device.
- **Video settings**: Turn your camera on/off or change resolution.
- **Layout options**: Switch between gallery and speaker view.
- **Call info**: See details like duration and participants.

> 🎧 **Troubleshooting**: If your audio sounds fuzzy, try switching to a different input device in the settings.

---

## Mastering the Call Toolbar: Your Control Center

The call toolbar is your one-stop shop for managing the call. Here’s what each button does:

| Icon | Name | Function |
|------|------|----------|
| 🎤 | Microphone | Mute/unmute your audio |
| 📹 | Camera | Turn your video on/off |
| 🖥️ | Screen | Share your screen |
| 👥 | People | View and manage participants |
| 🎶 | More | Access settings and layout options |
| 🚪 | Leave | End the call for yourself |

> 📌 **Pro Tip**: Press **Cmd+Shift+A (Mac)** or **Ctrl+Shift+A (Windows)** to quickly mute/unmute during a call.

### Keyboard Shortcuts to Save Time

Slack supports several shortcuts to make calls smoother:

- **M**: Mute/unmute
- **V**: Turn video on/off
- **S**: Start/stop screen sharing
- **Q**: Leave the call

> 💡 **Bonus**: You can find all keyboard shortcuts by pressing **Cmd+/ (Mac)** or **Ctrl+/ (Windows)** in Slack.

---

## Real-World Example: Fixing a Bug in 10 Minutes

Let’s walk through a realistic scenario where Slack Calls save the day.

**Scenario**: You’re a developer, and a teammate in the `#project-x` channel shares a bug report:
> *@here The login button isn’t redirecting users properly. Help!*

Instead of starting a long thread or scheduling a meeting, you decide to use a Huddle.

1. You click the **📞 phone icon** in the `#project-x` channel.
2. The Huddle starts, and your teammate joins within seconds.
3. You quickly explain the issue, but it’s hard to visualize. So, you click the **📹 camera icon** to turn on video.
4. Still not clear enough? You share your screen (🖥️) and show the button’s behavior.
5. Your teammate spots the missing `event.preventDefault()` in the JavaScript and fixes it on the spot.
6. You both leave the call. The bug is resolved in under 10 minutes—no emails, no meetings, no waiting.

This is the kind of seamless collaboration Slack Calls enable.

---

## Common Questions and Quick Fixes

### “I started a Huddle, but no one joined. Why?”
- They might be on **Do Not Disturb** or offline.
- Check their **presence indicator** (green dot = active, red = away).
- Send them a DM: *"Hey, can you join the Huddle in #project-x?"*

### “My audio isn’t working. What do I do?”
1. Click the **⋯** in the call toolbar.
2. Go to **Audio settings**.
3. Test your microphone and select a different input device if needed.

### “Can I record the call?”
Slack Huddles and Calls aren’t recorded by default. If you need a recording:
- Use a third-party app like **OBS** or **QuickTime Player** to screen-record.
- Or, summarize key points in a follow-up message in the channel.

> 🔒 **Privacy Note**: Always ask teammates before recording.

### “What if I accidentally leave the call?”
- You can rejoin by clicking the **Join** button in the notification or channel.
- If no one’s left, the Huddle ends automatically.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Slack Huddles** are instant voice calls that start with one click and end when everyone leaves—perfect for quick chats.
- You can **upgrade to a video call** anytime during a Huddle by clicking the camera icon.
- **Screen sharing** lets you show, not just tell, making collaboration faster and clearer.
- Use the **call toolbar** to control audio, video, participants, and layout—your control center for every call.
- **Keyboard shortcuts** and **accessibility settings** make calls smoother and more efficient.
- Huddles and Calls keep conversations **centralized in Slack**, reducing email clutter and scheduling delays.

You now have the tools to turn quick questions into instant answers, and vague messages into clear decisions—all without leaving Slack. Next time you’re tempted to send an email or schedule a meeting, consider starting a Huddle instead. Your future self (and your teammates) will thank you.

modules.title: Managing Your Availability and Status
modules.content:
## Why Your Status Matters More Than You Think

Imagine this: You’re deep in a complex project, your screen glowing with spreadsheets and code snippets. The deadline is tomorrow, and you’ve just realized a critical error. Frantically, you shoot off a message to your teammate. No response. Thirty minutes later, still nothing. Finally, you see their name pop up—*green*. They were online the whole time. But they were in a meeting. You didn’t know. Now the delay has cost the team precious hours.

This scenario isn’t hypothetical. Teams waste countless hours because people miss each other’s availability cues. Slack’s **status** feature isn’t just a cute emoji—it’s a productivity safeguard. It’s the difference between seamless collaboration and frustrating delays.

In this chapter, you’ll learn how to use your status to communicate your availability clearly, avoid unnecessary interruptions, and keep your team aligned without ever sending a follow-up message like *“Did you see my message?”*

---

## Understanding Presence and Status in Slack

Before diving into settings, it’s important to understand two key terms:

- **Presence indicator**: The small colored dot next to your name in Slack that shows whether you’re currently active (green), idle (yellow), or offline (gray). This updates automatically based on your activity, like typing or moving your mouse.
- **Status**: A custom message or emoji you set to give teammates more context about your availability, role, or focus. Unlike the presence indicator, which is automatic, your status is something you control.

Think of the presence indicator as a traffic light, and your status as the sign above it. The light tells people *if* you’re available. Your status tells them *why* or *how* to reach you.

### How Others See Your Status

When someone views your profile or hovers over your name in a channel or DM, they’ll see:
- Your **presence indicator** (green, yellow, or gray)
- Your **custom status message** (e.g., “In a meeting until 2 PM 🏃‍♂️”)
- The **time your status was set** (if it’s a temporary one)

This visibility helps teammates make smart decisions about when to message you or when to wait.

---

## Setting Your Status to Reflect Your Availability

Slack makes it easy to update your status in seconds. Here’s how:

1. Click your **profile picture** in the top-right corner of Slack.
2. Select **Set status** from the dropdown menu.
3. Choose from Slack’s **pre-set options**, or select **Set custom status** for more control.

The pre-set options include:
- **Active** (green)
- **Away** (yellow)
- **Do not disturb** (red)
- **Offline** (gray)

But you can go further.

---

## Using Status Emojis and Custom Status Messages

Status messages add context. Instead of just saying *“Active”*, you can say *“Deep in sprint planning 🏃‍♂️”* or *“Focused work until noon 🧠”*.

### How to Add an Emoji to Your Status
- After selecting **Set status**, type your message.
- Add an emoji by typing `:` followed by the emoji name (e.g., `:wave:`) or clicking the emoji picker.
- Press **Save**.

✅ **Example Statuses:**
- *“In a client call 📞”*
- *“Out for lunch 🍽️”*
- *“Working remotely 🏠”*
- *“Need focus time — message me only if urgent 🚨”*

⚠️ Avoid vague statuses like *“Busy”*. They don’t help teammates know *when* you’ll be available again.

---

## Making Statuses Temporary with “Clear After”

Slack’s “Clear after” feature lets you set a status that expires automatically—perfect for meetings, breaks, or focused work blocks.

### How to Use “Clear After”
1. Open **Set status** from your profile.
2. Type your message and emoji.
3. Click **Clear after** and choose a time:
   - 30 minutes
   - 1 hour
   - 2 hours
   - Custom time (up to 24 hours)
4. Click **Save**.

📌 **Example:**
You set *“In a team sync 📅”* and choose **Clear after: 1 hour**.
At 2:00 PM, you’ll return to your previous status automatically—no manual reset needed.

This prevents you from forgetting to update your status after a meeting ends.

---

## Setting a Custom Status for Projects or Timeframes

Some work spans days or weeks. A meeting status won’t cut it. That’s where **custom statuses** shine.

### When to Use a Custom Status
- You’re working on a specific project for a week.
- You’re on vacation or out of office.
- You’re leading a sprint or initiative.

✅ **Example:**
*“Working on Q2 Launch 🚀 — email for urgent issues”*
With a custom timeframe like **Clear after: 1 week**.

This tells teammates:
- What you’re doing
- How long you’ll be focused on it
- How to reach you in an emergency

---

## Scenario: Putting It All Together

**Alex**, a developer on the marketing team, is juggling two projects:
- A website redesign (due in 3 days)
- A quarterly report (due next week)

On Monday morning, Alex:
1. Sets a **custom status**: *“Coding sprint — Q2 site launch 💻”*, with **Clear after: 3 days**.
2. Takes a lunch break and sets *“Lunch break 🍽️”* with **Clear after: 1 hour**.
3. Joins a client call and updates to *“Client call 📞”*, clearing after **2 hours**.

Each status gives teammates context. No one messages Alex during the sprint. No one interrupts the client call. And when Alex returns from lunch, the status resets automatically.

Contrast that with a team where no one sets statuses:
- Messages pile up.
- Meetings get missed.
- Focus time is constantly broken.
- The cycle of *“Did you see my message?”* begins again.

---

## Best Practices for Managing Your Status

Here are some proven ways to use status effectively:

- **Update before you start something important** — not after.
- **Be specific** — “In a meeting” is better than “Busy”.
- **Use emojis sparingly** — they’re visual cues, not decoration.
- **Set a clear alternative** — if you’re unavailable, say where to go: *“Email me at alex@example.com ✉️”*.
- **Reset when done** — use “Clear after” to automate cleanup.

Remember: Your status isn’t just for you. It’s for your team. A well-maintained status reduces noise, respects focus, and builds trust.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Status Issues

Even with simple tools, things can go wrong.

### “My status won’t update”
- Make sure you’re not in **Do Not Disturb (DND)** mode. DND overrides status updates.
- Check your internet connection.
- Try refreshing Slack or logging out and back in.

### “My status shows as ‘Away’ even when I’m active”
- Slack’s idle timer starts after 30 minutes of inactivity. If you’re reading but not typing, you may appear away.
- Move your mouse or switch apps periodically during long reads.

### “Teammates don’t see my status”
- Ensure you’re in the same **workspace**.
- Confirm your status isn’t hidden due to privacy settings (rare in most workspaces).
- Ask a teammate to check if they see your updated status.

---

## Quick Reference: Status Commands

| Action | How to Do It |
|-------|---------------|
| Open status menu | Click profile picture → **Set status** |
| Set custom status | Type message + emoji → **Save** |
| Set temporary status | Choose **Clear after** and time → **Save** |
| Clear status manually | Click profile → **Clear status** |
| View someone’s status | Hover over their name in any channel |

---

## Ready to Be Seen Without Saying a Word

Your status is a silent collaborator. It speaks when you can’t. It guides teammates when you’re busy. It respects boundaries without saying no.

By mastering your status, you’re not just managing your availability—you’re managing the team’s expectations. And that’s a powerful productivity multiplier.

Next time you’re about to send a message, ask yourself:
*Could my teammate answer this better if they knew my status?*
If the answer is yes, update your status first.

Then send the message.

modules.title: Slack Etiquette and Best Practices for Teams
modules.content:
## Why Slack Etiquette Isn’t Just “Being Polite”

Imagine this: You wake up to 47 unread Slack messages. Half are unrelated to your work. One is a file attachment buried under 20 replies. Another mentions you in a channel you never joined. A third is a long-winded update that could have been a two-sentence summary. By noon, you’ve spent 45 minutes digging through the noise instead of focusing on your tasks.

That’s not Slack’s fault—and it’s not your fault either. It’s the result of *no etiquette*. Without clear rules, Slack turns from a productivity multiplier into a communication black hole.

Etiquette isn’t about being formal or stifling creativity. It’s about making sure your team’s communication is *effective*, *respectful*, and *actionable*. When used well, Slack can replace email, cut down on meetings, and keep everyone aligned. But without structure, it collapses under its own weight.

This chapter isn’t about decorum—it’s about survival. We’ll cover how to organize conversations so they don’t spiral, how to choose the right place to talk, and how to write messages that get answers (not sighs). Think of it as the user manual for human behavior in Slack.

---

## Organizing Work with Clear Channel Names and Structure

Channels are the backbone of Slack. They’re like designated rooms in a virtual office—each with a purpose. But if you name a channel `#random-ideas-for-the-website` and another `#website-project-2025`, people will get lost. Or worse, post in the wrong place.

### Why Channel Organization Matters

Unclear channels lead to:
- **Fragmented conversations**: People ask, “Wait, where was that discussed?”
- **No clear ownership**: No one knows who’s responsible for what.
- **Slow response times**: Messages get buried under unrelated chatter.

A well-organized workspace saves time and reduces frustration.

### Naming Conventions: Less Is More

Use **short, descriptive names** that everyone understands. Follow a consistent pattern.

**Good examples:**
- `#marketing-campaigns`
- `#engineering-backend`
- `#hr-recruiting`

**Avoid:**
- `#project-name-phase-2-final-final` (how many finals are there?)
- `#things-we-need-to-remember` (too vague)
- `#johns-idea-for-q3` (personal, not team-focused)

**Pro tip:** Add a prefix like `team-`, `project-`, or `topic-` if you have many channels. For example:
- `team-marketing`
- `project-launch-q4`
- `topic-ai-tools`

This helps people scan and understand context at a glance.

### Public vs. Private Channels: Know the Difference

- **Public channels** are open to everyone in the workspace. Use them for team-wide topics, project updates, or general announcements.
- **Private channels** are for sensitive or invite-only discussions (e.g., hiring, budgets, executive updates).

**When in doubt, default to public**—but only if the topic benefits from broader input. If it’s about a specific sub-team or confidential issue, go private.

**Never use private channels for gossip or exclusion.** Slack etiquette isn’t just about rules—it’s about respect.

### Archiving Old Channels

Channels that are inactive or outdated should be archived. This keeps the workspace clean and helps people focus on what matters.

**How to archive:**
1. Click the channel name at the top.
2. Select **Settings** > **Archive this channel**.
3. Confirm.

Archived channels can still be searched, so nothing is lost—but they won’t clutter your sidebar.

---

## Channels vs. Direct Messages: Know When to Use Each

It’s tempting to fire off a **Direct Message (DM)** every time you need to ask someone something. But DMs can become just as messy as channels if overused.

### When to Use a Channel
Use a **channel** when:
- The conversation involves **more than two people**.
- The topic **relates to a shared project or goal**.
- Others might **learn from or contribute** to the discussion.
- The information **needs to be searchable later**.

**Example:**
> “Hey team, the client feedback for the homepage redesign is in. Let’s review it in `#design-feedback`. Everyone’s welcome—we’ll discuss at 3pm.”

### When to Use a DM
Use a **DM** when:
- You need a **quick, private answer** from one person.
- The topic is **personal or sensitive**.
- You’re **coordinating directly** with someone (e.g., scheduling a call).

**Example:**
> “Hey Alex, can you send me the latest API specs? I need them for the integration.”

### The DM Spiral: How It Starts, How It Ends

One DM leads to another. Then another. Soon, you’ve got 20 parallel conversations cluttering your sidebar. People miss messages. Context gets lost.

**Avoid the spiral by:**
- Starting in a **channel** if others might benefit.
- Using **threads** even in DMs to keep topics separate.
- Summarizing key points in a **channel** afterward if needed.

---

## Threads: Your Secret Weapon for Clean Conversations

Threads are like side conversations inside a message. They keep replies organized without creating new channels or DMs.

### Why Use Threads?
- **Reduces noise**: Main messages stay clean.
- **Improves focus**: People can follow the main topic and opt into side discussions.
- **Makes searching easier**: Thread replies are searchable along with the original message.

**Example:**
> **Main message:** “Team, the client meeting is at 2pm. Agenda attached.”
> - *Thread reply 1:* “Can we add the QA timeline to the agenda?”
> - *Thread reply 2:* “I’ll send the latest mockups by 1pm.”

Without threads, this becomes a chain of 20 replies, burying the original message.

### Best Practices for Threads
- **Reply in threads**, not in the main channel.
- **Pin important replies** if they contain key info.
- **Mention someone in the thread** if they need to respond.
- **Don’t hijack threads**: If your reply changes the topic entirely, start a new message.

**Common mistake:** Posting a new message in response to a thread reply, creating a parallel conversation. This fragments the discussion.

---

## Writing Clear, Concise Messages That Get Responses

A well-written message is like a good elevator pitch: short, clear, and to the point. But in Slack, people often default to rambling—especially when they’re busy or emotional.

### The 3-Part Message Formula
Every message should have:
1. **Context** – What’s the situation?
2. **Action** – What do you need?
3. **Deadline** (if needed) – When is this due?

**Example (Good):**
> “Hi team, the client wants to see the homepage redesign by EOD Friday. Can we review the latest mockups in `#design-feedback` by 3pm today? Thanks!”

**Example (Bad):**
> “Hey I was just thinking about the website and the client said they need something soon and I was wondering if we could maybe look at the mockups and I think the color scheme is off but I’m not sure if anyone else noticed and—”

That second one might be slightly exaggerated—but you’ve seen variations of it.

### Be Specific with Your Ask
- ❌ “Can someone help with this?”
- ✅ “Can Priya help with the login flow? She’s the backend owner.”

### Use Bullet Points or Numbered Lists for Complex Info

**Good:**
> “Here are the three priorities for Q4:
> 1. Fix the mobile checkout bug
> 2. Launch the new dashboard
> 3. Document the API changes
>
> Let me know which one you’d like to tackle first.”

**Bad:**
> “We have a lot of things to do for Q4 like fix the mobile checkout which is really important and the new dashboard needs to launch soon and also we need to document the API changes that’s all.”

### Avoid “Hey” Messages

A message that just says “Hey” or “Hi” forces the recipient to respond before they know what’s needed. This creates unnecessary friction.

**Instead:**
> “Hi Alex, can you review the pull request by 5pm? Thanks!”

---

## Mentioning the Right People at the Right Time

The **@mention** is powerful—but it’s also easy to abuse.

### When to @mention Someone
- You need their **specific input or decision**.
- You’re **assigning them a task**.
- You’re **directly referencing them** in a discussion.

### When *Not* to @mention Someone
- To get their attention for something **unrelated**.
- To vent or complain (use a DM or talk in person).
- Just to say “hello” or make a comment they don’t need.

**Pro tip:** Use **@channel** or **@here** sparingly. These notify *everyone* in the channel and can cause notification overload.

- **@channel** – Use for urgent, team-wide announcements (e.g., “Server down!”).
- **@here** – Use for urgent messages when only active members need to respond (e.g., “Quick sync needed in 10 mins”).

Avoid using them for non-urgent updates.

**Example of misuse:**
> “@channel FYI we’re switching to Zoom for calls now.”

This interrupts everyone’s workflow. A better approach:
> “Heads up: We’re moving to Zoom. Join the huddle at 2pm for a quick walkthrough. #team-meetings”

---

## Common Slack Etiquette Pitfalls—and How to Avoid Them

### 1. The “Reply All” Problem
Slack doesn’t have a “Reply All” button—but people still do it by replying to every recipient in a DM thread instead of creating a group DM.

**Fix:** Create a **group DM** for multiple people:
1. Click the **pencil icon** in the DM sidebar.
2. Add multiple people.
3. Name the group (e.g., “Marketing Launch Team”).

This keeps conversations organized and avoids cluttering individual DMs.

### 2. The “File Dump” Issue
Attaching files without context or naming them “Screenshot.png” leads to chaos.

**Fix:**
- Name files clearly: `“2025-Q4-Marketing-Plan.pdf”`
- Add a **caption** in the message: “Here’s the updated marketing plan with the new budget.”

### 3. The “Silent Treatment” Response
Ignoring messages or leaving people hanging without a response (even if you’re busy) is rude.

**Fix:**
- Send a quick reply: “Got it—will review by tomorrow.”
- Use **status updates** to signal availability: “In meetings until 3pm—replying after.”

### 4. The “Async Meeting” Trap
Some teams default to Slack for everything—even long, detailed discussions that would be better in a call.

**Fix:**
- Use a **Slack Huddle** or **call** for complex or emotional topics.
- Reserve channels for async updates and decisions.

### 5. The “Status Confusion” Problem
Leaving your status on “Available” when you’re actually in deep work—or setting it to “Away” when you’re just grabbing lunch—leads to frustration.

**Fix:**
- Update your status with context: “Focus time—replying after 2pm” or “On vacation—back Oct 5.”

---

## Real-World Scenario: A Slack Etiquette Success Story

**Situation:** The marketing team is preparing a campaign launch. They’ve set up these channels:
- `#marketing-campaigns`
- `#design-feedback`
- `#content-review`

**What happened:**
- The campaign manager posted the creative brief in `#marketing-campaigns`.
- The designer replied in a **thread**, asking for clarification on the brand voice.
- The copywriter added a thread reply with three headline options.
- The social media manager tagged the campaign manager in the thread: “@Jane, can we finalize the CTAs by EOD?”
- Jane pinned the final assets in the channel and announced the launch timeline.

Result: Everyone stayed aligned. No emails. No missed messages. No confusion.

**Key takeaways from this scenario:**
- Used **channels for visibility**.
- Used **threads for organization**.
- Used **mentions for action items**.
- Used **pins for clarity**.

---

## Final Thought: Slack Is a Tool, Not a Lifeline

Slack isn’t meant to replace all communication. It’s meant to **reduce friction**, not create it.

The best teams use Slack as a **central hub**—not the only place they talk. They combine channels with Huddles, calls, and in-person chats when needed.

Remember:
- **Channels** = shared spaces.
- **Threads** = clean side conversations.
- **DMs** = private, focused asks.
- **Status** = your availability.
- **Mentions** = targeted attention.

Use these tools wisely—and your team will spend less time sorting messages and more time building great things.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Name channels clearly and consistently** — use short, descriptive names with prefixes (e.g., `#team-marketing`) to keep things organized.
- **Use public channels by default** — reserve private channels for sensitive or limited-access discussions.
- **Archive old or inactive channels** — keep your workspace clean and focused.
- **Choose channels over DMs when others might benefit** — don’t default to DMs for group topics.
- **Always use threads for replies** — keep main messages clean and searchable.
- **Follow the 3-part message formula** — include context, action, and deadline (if needed).
- **Mention people only when necessary** — avoid @channel and @here unless urgent.
- **Keep messages concise** — avoid “Hey” messages and long-winded updates.
- **Update your status regularly** — help others know when you’re available or busy.
- **Combine Slack with other tools** — use Huddles, calls, or in-person chats for complex or sensitive topics.
